1.b: The end of January saw one of the year’s strongest projects right off the bat. With PXL DEX, Kim Asendorf extends his experiments with pixels and blockchains by ratcheting up the complexity, treating the pixel as both material and asset.

2.b: A member of Jeffrey Steele’s Systems Group (1969) and a former member of the British Constructivists, Wise was a prominent example of a systems artist, like Vera Molnar, moving from systematic thinking to programmed art with computers.

3.b: “Ross Goodwin writes 1 the Road, an experimental AI-powered novel. Inspired by Jack Kerouac’s On the Road, Goodwin drives from New York to New Orleans accompanied by an AI program trained on poetry and sci-fi text corpora, plus a FourSquare data set.

4.b: Founded by John Warnock and Charles Geschke, Adobe Systems in 1984 unveiled PostScript, a groundbreaking page description language and computer graphics technology that played a pivotal role in the history of digital art and graphic design, used by artists such as Mark Wilson.

5.t: Energized Artscience at the Chicago Museum of Science and Industry
5.b: Curated by pioneer, Sonia Landy Sheridan who also wrote the show catalog, this exhibition at the Museum of Science and Industry does not have much existing information about it. Anymore would be greatly appreciated.

6.b: Eden is an interactive, self-generating, artificial ecosystem installation active from 2004–2012. McCormack created artificial creatures that inhabited a virtual world governed by minimal physics, seeking survival through adaptation and learning.

7.b: Named by 1921 and led by Vladimir Tatlin and Alexander Rodchenko, Constructivism is arguably the most influential movement of the first half of the 20th c. on digital and generative art.

8.t: Pour une peinture expérimentale programmée, in Groupe de recherche d’art visuel (Paris: Galerie Denise René; GRAV)
8.b: In the catalogue for this early GRAV exhibition, Morellet would spell out the group’s relevance to the programmed, digital generative art of today.

9.b: In October, Mario Klingemann launched Botto, a decentralized autonomous artist governed by a DAO (Decentralized Autonomous Organization).

10.t: I. J. Good Speaks on Machine Judgment at the Gaberbocchus Common Room
10.b: As described by Jasia Reichardt herself at Le Random (“The Ultraintelligent Machine and Gaberbocchus Common Room”), on January 14, 1958, the mathematician I. J. Good, a one-time colleague of Alan Turing, spoke at the Gaberbocchus Common Room in London.

11.t: Molnár’s Paris: Rue Hallé Permanent Home
11.b: In 1964, the Molnárs planned and constructed their own three-story home and studio on Rue Hallé. Vera later reminisced, “It was the Morellets who lent us money, plus the family and the bank, which meant that we were poor all our lives.”

12.t: Grand tir–séance Galerie J by Niki de Saint Phalle
12.b: This convention-defying work of chance art saw Saint Phalle create an assemblage of white, found objects, surrounded by sacks of colored paint. She would then fire a rifle at the paint sacks to explosively create the work.

13.t: Douglas Hofstadter’s Publishes Book Gödel, Escher, Bach: An Eternal Golden Braid
13.b: This book exploring the latest trends in math, logic and computer language, would greatly influence artist Roman Verostko.

14.b: Exhibited at Cybernetic Serendipity, this ahead of its time cybernetic sculpture anticipated interactivity in electronic art.

15.b: In November, Refik Anadol unveiled Unsupervised at the Museum of Modern Art (MoMA), a groundbreaking AI-driven installation that reimagines over 200 years of the museum’s collection.

16.t: Landscapes and Nude Portraits by Robbie Barrat
16.b: In 2017 Robbie Barrat began using Generative Adversarial Networks to make art, producing his first two significant bodies of work, Landscapes and Nude Portraits, which reached collectors in 2018.

17.t: Apple’s Lisa: Early Personal Computer with GUI
17.b: Developed by Apple, the Lisa was one of the first commercial personal computers with a GUI (Graphical User Interface). Lisa was short for “Local Integrated Software Architecture” as well as the name of Apple co-founder Steve Jobs’s daughter.

18.b: We open January 2021 with a bang. This consequential deep learning model designed by OpenAI “generates”—as in creates—digital images from natural language descriptions.

19.b: Despite legal action that delayed Tezos’s initial release by nearly a year, the chain officially launched on mainnet on September 17, 2018. The project was watched closely, as it had been one of the largest ICOs at the time.

20.t: Super Mario Clouds by Cory Arcangel
20.b: In a masterpiece of video game art, Cory Arcangel deconstructs a familiar cultural artifact, reducing the iconic Super Mario Brothers game to its ethereal background only.

21.b: Curated by Christiane Paul and indicative of the early millennium enthusiasm for digital art—as the Internet sucked more and more of the cultural air—New York’s Whitney Museum hosted two major digital themed exhibitions in 2001 with Data Dynamics (March 2001) and BitStreams.

22.b: In April, SuperRare, one of the oldest surviving crypto art marketplaces, launched its beta smart contract on the Ethereum blockchain.

23.b: This landmark, hugely influence piece of chance music consists of a graphic score of transparent sheets the performer superimposes to derive a realisation.

24.t: Computer/Culture 83 at La Chartreuse de Villeneuve in Avignon, France
24.b: Computer/Culture 83 was organized by C.I.R.C.A (Centre International de Recherche, de Création et d’Animation) at La Chartreuse de Villeneuve in Avignon, France.

25.t: First Symposium on Small Computers in the Arts Held in Philadelphia
25.b: Held from 20 to 22 November 1981 and sponsored by the Philadelphia Area Computer Society, the University of Pennsylvania and the IEEE, the symposium would become an annual event and an important gathering of American computer artists in the 1980s.

26.b: First truly personal computers to sell in large numbers. It was available in 1975 for $397 as a kit and appeared on the January 1975 cover of Popular Electronics.

27.t: Art and the Computer at the Worcester Art Museum and Computer Generated Art Exhibit at Old Dominion University
27.b: These events held in the United States were “some of the most important computer graphics exhibitions of the last years,” according to Herbert W. Franke in Computer Graphics, Computer Art (1985).

28.t: Gyorgy Kepes Establishes the Center for Advanced Visual Studies (CAVS) at MIT
28.b: The Center was established at The Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) by Kepes “to bring artists from around the world to collaborate with MIT’s community of scientists and engineers, [in order] to produce works using new directions in technological approach.”

29.t: ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge
29.b: This competition would play an out-sized role in this story, as the little-known event was responsible for the decade’s most important machine vision breakthrough in 2012, when deep convolutional neural networks, a technique first built in the 1980s, won the competition outright.

30.t: Art ware: Kunst und Elektronik at Messe AG and Siemens AG, Hannover, Germany
30.b: Premiering in 1986, this exhibition of mostly German electronic artists would continue annually until 1990.

31.t: Image World at the Whitney Museum of American Art
31.b: This influential exhibition, which is accompanied by essays by Marvin Heiferman, Lisa Phillips and John G. Hanhardt, captures the essence of the “Image World.”
